catalog_quote: 0.3.2. Stress. Stress normally occurs on the first syllable of a word, which may have up to four syllables. Some exceptions are noted below: (a) The vowel /ɨ/ is never stressed unless the only vowels in the word are /e/ or another /ɨ/. Examples are: (1) mɨ́tɨk man (2) mɨ́te woman (3) hɨ́ne knife (4) k-ɨ́rɨr he-flees (5) k-ɨsáwɨn he-hides (6) k-átɨp he-talks (b) The vowel /e/ is never stressed unless the only other vowels are /ɨ/ or another /e/. Examples are: (7) népere dog (8) pérpere flying fox (9) k-ewát he-gives (10) k-ekíntɨp he-steals ... [vowel chart, same page:] mid central close unrounded : /ʌ/ symbolised /e/ ... [0.3 Presentation, p.218:] an inventory of Au phonemes is given first, followed by comments on stress (which is predictable)

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page image we hold of Scorza 1985 p.219 (sec. 0.3.2), vowel chart and p.218 'predictable' remark included. (2) The deciding source is a 1985 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch by the long-term SIL fieldworker; its stress note is brief but explicit, with stress-marked examples showing central-vowel avoidance (mɨ́tɨk vs k-ɨsáwɨn, k-ewát, k-ekíntɨp), which is exactly what the 'weight / full-vs-reduced-vowel, left edge' coding encodes. Nothing later and primary exists: Glottolog's descriptive list is all Scorza 1971-1985, and the only post-1985 linguistic work located (Elgh 2023, LLM 41) cites Scorza 1985:219 for first-syllable stress. (3) downloaded now via the Internet Archive: Scorza's dedicated phonemes ms (1971, rev. Nov 1973). Its sec. 5.3.1 (typed p.16) says stress is non-contrastive, cued by loudness and high pitch, 'usually' on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words, 1

sources.quote: 'Stress is not contrastive phonemically. It usually occurs on third syllable of a four syllable word, the first syllable on a three syllable word, and alternates from syllable to syllable on two syllable words, that is from initial or final depending on the word. Stress is recognized by loudness and high pitch. Tone is not phonemically pertinent, nor is pitch.' No mention of vowel quality conditioning stress.
sources.locator: section 5.3.1 'Phonemic Status of Stress, Tone and Pitch', typed PAGE 16 = PDF page 17
sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Au; gives stress cues (loudness + high pitch) and an earlier placement statement (3rd syllable in 4-syllable words, variable in disyllables) that differs from the 1985 'first syllable, up to four syllables' default our record quotes; worth citing as a secondary source/caution.
